newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Chirac faces landmark decision on NATO.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Chirac faces landmark decision on NATO.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac faces probably the most important strategic decision of his presidency in the coming weeks on whether to take France back into the military wing of a reformed NATO alliance.
His choice could affect the development of the U.S.-led alliance and of a European defence identity almost as profoundly as General Charles de Gaulle's 1966 decision to pull France out.

Yet the outcome is uncertain, with French ministers warning publicly that unless the United States yields a fairer share of NATO commands to the Europeans in time for a landmark summit in Madrid in July, France may well stay out for now.

Because it is a question of NATO's internal reform, the dispute between Paris and Washington will not be on the agenda at this week's U.S.-Russian summit in Helsinki. But it is part of a package, including NATO enlargement, which is supposed to be approved at Madrid.

The high-stakes poker game between Paris and Washington over the "Europeanisation" of NATO has come to focus on who holds the southern regional command which controls the Mediterranean and thus access to the Balkans, North Africa and the Middle East.

Chirac, who sees himself as De Gaulle's spiritual heir, began a rapprochement with NATO shortly after his election in 1995, drawing the lessons from predecessor Francois Mitterrand's failure to build a European defence independent of the alliance.

He sent his defence minister to NATO meetings for the first time since the alliance was forced to uproot its headquarters from Paris, Versailles, and Fontainebleau and move to Belgium in 1967 in the most serious crisis in its 48-year history.

But Chirac made a full return to NATO's integrated military command, which plans, trains and conducts joint operations, conditional on a greater role for the European allies in the 16-nation bloc, long dominated by Washington.

He raised the stakes with two assertive letters to U.S. President Bill Clinton last year declaring the tug-of-war over the AFSOUTH command in Naples to be of "capital importance". The United States told France firmly to forget it.

"President Chirac put himself in a very difficult position because if he goes ahead with integration without gaining satisfaction, he will be criticised, and if he stops, he'll be criticised too," said Pascal Boniface, director of the IRIS strategic research institute.
FRENCH SEEK EURO POWER, U.S. ARGUES MILITARY EFFICIENCY

The French say the Europeans should run the southern region because Americans hold both NATO strategic commands, the Supreme Allied Commander in Europe (SACEUR) based in Mons, Belgium, and the supreme Atlantic commander (SACLANT) in Norfolk, Virgina.

Putting a European in charge, they argue, would be a visible sign that the European allies were at last taking responsibility for their own security in the area where many of the challenges to stability in the early 21st century loom.

Besides, say the French, Washington has more than halved its troop presence in Europe to 100,000 since the end of the Cold War and is increasingly reluctant to see its forces embroiled in minor conflicts on the fringes of Europe.
The United States retorts that it still has the biggest military capabilities in the area, notably the nuclear-armed Sixth Fleet, whose commanding admiral has traditionally headed AFSOUTH.

It also points to its role as Middle East peace broker, its stabilising influence in the chronic feuds between NATO partners Greece and Turkey, and its decisive intervention to end the war in Bosnia to buttress its case.
U.S. officials say Congress, tempted by unilateralism since the collapse of the Soviet Union, would be less committed to NATO and to Mediterranean security under a European command.
Some also say France should not be rewarded just for coming back after having been NATO's gadfly for 30 years.
With the notable exception of Germany, few European allies support the French case, although most are keen to see Paris back in the fold and thus hope to find a face-saving deal.

After the American rebuff, the French lowered their sights, suggesting the command rotate among U.S. and European officers or be split along functional or geographical lines -- between air-naval and ground forces, or between east and west.

Washington ruled out most of these ideas as militarily impractical, but it has at least begun to negotiate. NATO aides say one problem is that after three decades on the sidelines, the French do not understand how the alliance works.
"They seemed to believe that troops assigned to NATO were given away completely by national governments," one alliance official said.
GERMANS OFFER COMPROMISE, CHIRAC LOOKS TO CLINTON

Diplomats said U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen, who toured Europe this month, embraced a compromise plan that would pledge a review of the AFSOUTH issue after five or six years and meanwhile give the Europeans a deputy southern commander and a new rapid-reaction force for the Western Mediterranean.
But to the dismay of Germany, which had invested political capital to sell the formula to Washington, Paris turned it down, seeking an immediate visible sharing of power on an equal level.

"The French position is unrealistic. That either means Chirac has decided he can't return to NATO for now for domestic reasons, or he thinks he can still charm Clinton," said a European diplomat involved in the talks.
"It's a poker game, but the Americans are better at poker than the French, and they hold the better cards," he said.
Talks are continuing and aides say Chirac will take his decision in May, well before Madrid.

Washington has already accepted the principle of a European deputy supreme commander who would head a European chain of command to run military operations which the United States chose not to join, using NATO assets if the alliance agreed.

French officials say that if the Americans go the extra mile, they can win the prize of a reunited, "re-balanced" NATO, a new partnership with Russia and a painless enlargement of the alliance to former communist East European states.
U.S. officials say they would like to have the French, whose willingness to deploy forces to world troublespots Washington admires, back in the NATO fold, but not at any price.
Paris would only be punishing itself if it stayed out, they add. A European defence identity would evolve within NATO anyway, and France would be marginalised.
FRENCH MILITARY WANTS IN, LEFT WANTS OUT
After public rows with Washington, the French government has played down the NATO issue, saying publicly it will be no big deal if France stays where it is now.

Among those keenest for full NATO membership are France's generals, dismayed to realise in the Gulf War that their forces were in the second division of Western military, less well equipped and ill-prepared to operate with allies.

The professionalisation of the French armed forces, decreed by Chirac last year, is partly intended to remedy those defects, but it will leave fewer jobs for senior officers, who therefore look to NATO posts to salvage their careers.
"NATO is where the military planning of the major powers happens. Not being there is an increasing handicap," said a colonel in the French general staff.

Among those most fiercely opposed are nationalists such as former Socialist defence minister Jean-Pierre Chevenement, who argues that if France survived the Cold War without its forces being integrated into NATO, there is even less reason to return today, when Europe faces no pressing military threat.
"We would be surrendering to American hegemony, just as we are surrendering to German hegemony in the march to a single European currency," Chevenement said.
His view is shared by many old guard Gaullists in Chirac's own RPR party, weaned on rivalry with the United States, as well as by the Communists and the extreme-right National Front.

Distrust of NATO still runs deep in France's foreign policy establishment. Thierry de Montbrial, director of the French Institute for International Relations, calls the alliance "one of the fundamental instruments of...American imperial power".
The opposition Socialists, while not opposed in principle to reintegration, accuse Chirac of bungling the negotiations by agreeing to go back without getting anything in return.
"The Americans won't yield on the basic issue, so the whole thing is to find a face-saving solution that can be sold in France," Boniface said.
Diplomats on both sides say the odds are that Chirac will declare victory and rejoin, but no one is quite sure.
